I Noticed you haven't selected a hand guard yet. I just received mine for my 6.8 project. I chose a Midwest Industries Generation one hand guard. Since I want my 6.8 to be a tack driver I chose a free floating hand guard to remove and stress on the barrel and also allow for optimal barrel harmonics. Like every thing else there are pro's and con's to the the product.

First the Pro's. Since I am shooting from a 20 inch barrel the hand guard is a 15 inch model. It appears to be well built with machined 6061 aircraft grade aluminum. It has full rails on top and bottom and both sides which makes the hand guard very rigid. With my barrel profile the hand guard has about 1/2 to 5/8's air jacket around the barrel for cooling. There are 1/2 inch diameter closely spaced holes between the rails for lots of air circulation. The best thing I like is the mounting system. Midwest uses a special barrel nut with both interior and exterior threading. The barrel nut is about two inches long. Half way between the exterior threading is a groove cut with interior teeth.

To install the hand guard you install the barrel nut and cinch it up to specified torque. 35-45 Foot Pounds for most rifles. Then you screw on the hand guard jamb nut. The jam nut is the same size as the hand guard but only 3/8's inch wide. The threads for the hand guard are very close set, (Probably 50 tpi) so you have to be careful screwing it on to not cross thread it. You screw the hand guard all the way down until the tang of the top rail meets or comes in contact with the rail on top of the receiver. If it comes in contact you cannot screw it in any farther so you have to back it off until the tang on the top hand guard will align with the tang on the receiver. (Oh I suppose you could use a file and remove some metal on the hand guard tang to get it to match up but why remove the finish when it probably doesn't make and difference.) Any way once the hand guard top rail is properly aligned with the receiver rail, you screw the jamb nut down on the hand guard with the jamb nut wrench that they include with the hand guard. (Probably about 10-15 foot pounds should do it) Lastly you install the anti rotation screw in the screw hole at the bottom. (Remember that groove with teeth I mentioned. ) The tip of the anti rotation screw fits between the teeth in the groove. (Also Midwest includes lock-tight compound for all the anti rotation screw and probably the jamb nut and hand guard. )

When the hand guard is installed it is rock solid and you can hang sling studs, flash lights, and a bipod on it with out any problem.

Now for the con and it may be a big one. With the rails on both sides and bottom of the hand guard it is rather bulky and may not fit properly with a small hand. Also the sharp edges of the rail will be rough on hands if you do a lot of shooting. I think I will wear a shooting glove with it.

However Midwest does give you a free mouse pad!!!!!!!
